article.overview: A laser retroreflector array is a passive optical instrument made of many precisely shaped corner-cube prisms. Each corner cube returns an incoming laser beam back along its own path toward the source. On the Moon, arrays placed by the Apollo 11, 14 and 15 missions, by the Soviet Lunokhod rovers and, more recently, by the Chang'e-6 lander allow ground stations on Earth to fire short laser pulses at them and time the returning light. This Lunar Laser Ranging technique measures the Earth-Moon distance with very high precision and gives fixed reference points against which other measurements can be compared. The reflection itself needs no electrical power. The main limitations are the weakness of the returning signal, which depends on cube size, cube count and alignment, and thermal distortion of the cubes during the lunar day [1][2].
article.description: A retroreflector is an optical device that returns light to its source. A corner cube, the basic element used here, is a solid glass prism with three mutually perpendicular reflecting faces, so a beam entering the cube is reflected back in the direction it came from over a useful range of entry angles. An array groups many corner cubes into one panel so that the total returned light is larger than a single cube could give. The Apollo arrays use fused silica cubes 3.8 cm in diameter, arranged in grids on an aluminium panel [1][2]. Cube count, size and layout differ between missions, and so do their thermal and alignment behaviour. Because the arrays are passive, they transmit nothing of their own. The observing station supplies the laser, and the returned light is what it measures.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of a lunar laser retroreflector array is to let Earth-based observatories measure the distance to a fixed point on the Moon. A station fires a short laser pulse, the array returns some of the light, and the round-trip time is recorded. Repeated measurements to several arrays build a long record of the Earth-Moon distance [1]. The Apollo 15 array is the main target for laser ranging, and NASA describes it as one of four working retroreflector arrays on the Moon [3]. Later designs aim to improve the precision of the measurements. A design study by Turyshev and colleagues proposes a single large-aperture cube with a target single-pulse range precision of 1 mm [4]. The Chang'e-6 INRRI was described by its authors as an absolute control point for lunar geodesy, surface mapping and orbit determination [5].
article.operating_principle: A laser ranging station on Earth directs a short, intense laser pulse toward the Moon. Only a small fraction of the light reaches the array, and only a small fraction of that is returned to the station, because the beam spreads over a very large distance. The station records the time between sending the pulse and detecting the return, and the distance follows from the speed of light. The corner-cube geometry is what sends the return back toward the station rather than scattering it. Because the returned signal is weak, the cube size, number and alignment of an array strongly affect how much light comes back. The Turyshev design study notes that the small cubes of existing arrays spread the return timing when libration tilts them relative to Earth [4]. Libration is the apparent wobble of the Moon, which changes how much of the array faces Earth at a given time.
article.scientific_importance: Observatories have regularly ranged the Moon with these reflectors [1], so the arrays provide a long-running record of Earth-Moon distance measurements. Each array is a fixed point on the lunar surface whose position can be measured repeatedly from Earth. The Apollo 15 array is the main target for laser ranging, and NASA describes it as one of four working retroreflector arrays on the Moon [3]. The sources read do not quantify the scientific results derived from these measurements, so this article does not give values for them.

physical_specifications.note: There is no single universal specification for a laser retroreflector array. The values below are tied to named arrays and sources. The Turyshev design is a proposal and has no measured specification in the source read. Chang'e-6 INRRI values are limited to what the abstract read reports.

examples.name: Apollo 11 laser ranging retroreflector array
examples.type: Flown lunar instrument (Apollo 11, Sea of Tranquility)
examples.status: Flown and deployed on the lunar surface. The ILRS page states that observatories have regularly ranged the Moon with the Apollo reflectors. The page does not give a separate operating status for this array.
examples.array_layout: 10 x 10 grid of corner cubes (UCSD summary table)
examples.panel_size: 46 cm aluminium panel per the ILRS page; 0.45 m square per the UCSD summary table
examples.thermal_design: The ILRS page states that the array was designed to minimise thermal gradients across the cubes as the Moon's phase changes, which prevents thermal distortion from significantly reducing returned light.
examples.qualification: Not stated in the sources read.

examples.name: Apollo 14 laser ranging retroreflector array

examples.panel_size: Not separately stated in the sources read
examples.thermal_design: Described as identical to the Apollo 11 array in the ILRS page summary and as very similar in the UCSD summary table. Neither source gives separate thermal figures.
examples.qualification: Not stated in the sources read.

examples.name: Lunokhod 1 and Lunokhod 2 retroreflector arrays
examples.type: Flown lunar instruments carried by the Lunokhod rovers (associated with the Luna 17 and Luna 21 missions)
examples.status: Flown. The UCSD summary states that both arrays are now used routinely. Lunokhod 2's array continues to return signals. Lunokhod 1's array was not seen after the early 1970s until it was rediscovered in April 2010 using Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter images.
examples.corner_cube_material: Not stated in the sources read
examples.array_layout: Triangular corner cubes in a triangular configuration (UCSD summary table); French-built per the ILRS page
examples.panel_size: Each reflector 11 cm per side and total package 44 cm long by 19 cm across, as stated in the UCSD summary table. The UCSD summary does not clarify whether 11 cm refers to each triangular face or to the whole reflector.
examples.thermal_design: The UCSD summary states that returns are about 30 times weaker in lunar daylight than at lunar night, due to thermal distortion from the large cubes. It does not say whether this applies to both arrays. Lunokhod 2's array is about five times weaker than its twin.
examples.qualification: Not stated in the sources read.

examples.name: Chang'e-6 INRRI laser retroreflector
examples.type: Flown on the Chang'e-6 lander, which touched down in the Apollo basin on 2 June 2024 (per the 2025 abstract read)
examples.status: Installed on the top panel of the lander. The abstract read does not state whether INRRI has been activated, is operating, or has returned ranging data. The paper's authors describe it as the first laser retroreflector on the lunar far side, and the abstract reports no ranging or detection results.
examples.array_layout: Not stated in the abstract read
examples.panel_size: Not stated in the abstract read
examples.thermal_design: Not stated in the abstract read. The abstract says environmental qualification tests were run for the far-side surface, without giving results.
examples.qualification: The abstract says environmental qualification tests were conducted for the far-side surface. Results are not given in the abstract.

examples.panel_size: Not stated in the abstract read

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Panel and array sizes differ by design. The Apollo 11 and 14 arrays have a 46 cm aluminium panel per the ILRS page (0.45 m square per the UCSD summary table). The Apollo 15 array measures 105 x 65 cm per NASA. The Lunokhod package is 44 cm long by 19 cm across per the UCSD summary table. Chang'e-6 INRRI dimensions are not stated in the abstract read. The Turyshev design dimensions are not stated in the abstract read.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass is not stated in the ILRS or UCSD pages read, and the Apollo 15 Preliminary Science Report that may give it could not be extracted in this run. Apollo array masses are therefore recorded as null. The Chang'e-6 INRRI mass is not in the abstract read. A secondary search summary citing an arXiv paper gives a figure that was not verified, so no value is recorded here. The Turyshev concept is described only as low in mass, to allow robotic deployment, without a value [4].
physical_specifications.power_requirements: The reflection itself is passive and needs no electrical power. No power requirement is stated for any array in the sources read. The Chang'e-6 lander power arrangement is not described in the abstract read.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: The arrays sit on the lunar surface, exposed to vacuum, micrometeoroid impacts and large temperature swings between lunar day and night. These are general lunar conditions rather than values from a cited specification. The main environmental effect identified in the sources read is thermal distortion. The UCSD summary attributes the much weaker daytime returns of the Lunokhod arrays to thermal distortion of their large cubes [2]. The Apollo 11 array was designed to minimise thermal gradients across its cubes as the lunar phase changes [1]. Orientation toward Earth is also an operational factor, because libration changes how the arrays are tilted relative to Earth [4].
article.limitations: The returned signal from a retroreflector array is weak, and the strength of the return depends on cube size, count and alignment. The UCSD summary reports that the Apollo 15 array returned 6,300 of 8,400 range measurements (75%) as of 1994 [2]. Lunokhod returns are about 30 times weaker in lunar daylight than at night, and Lunokhod 2's array is about five times weaker than its twin [2]. The Turyshev design study states that degraded existing arrays still give useful but much weaker return signals [4]. The Chang'e-6 INRRI abstract reports no ranging results [5]. Each array is a single fixed point and does not map the Moon by itself.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: The Apollo, Lunokhod and Chang'e-6 arrays were carried to the Moon as parts of larger lunar missions. The Apollo arrays were placed on the surface by the crews, as the Apollo 15 image caption indicates [3]. The Lunokhod arrays were carried on rovers associated with the Luna 17 and Luna 21 missions [2]. The Chang'e-6 INRRI was installed on the top panel of the lander [5].
transportation_process: Integrate the array onto the spacecraft, lander or rover on Earth, with its mounting and orientation fixed before launch.
Launch the spacecraft and transfer it toward the Moon.
Deliver the array to the surface, either on a lander or carried by a rover.
Deploy or place the array so that its reflecting faces can be directed toward Earth. The Apollo 15 caption indicates that the array was placed on the surface by an astronaut [3].
Verify the array's position and orientation, because libration changes the array's tilt relative to Earth [4].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The Apollo arrays were placed by the crews [3]. The Lunokhod arrays were carried on rovers [2]. The Chang'e-6 INRRI was installed on the lander's top panel [5]. The sources read do not describe the deployment procedure for each array in detail.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo 11, 14 and 15 arrays, the Lunokhod 1 and 2 arrays, the Chang'e-6 INRRI, and the single-cube concept proposed by Turyshev and colleagues are the examples considered here.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: This article does not assert compatibility with any specific lander, rover or spacecraft. Compatibility would depend on mass, dimensions, mounting interface, orientation requirements, thermal behaviour and the deployment method. None of these were verified for a named lander in the sources read.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo 11, 14 and 15 arrays and the Lunokhod 1 and 2 arrays form the basis of decades of lunar laser ranging. Lunokhod 1's array was not detected after the early 1970s until it was rediscovered in April 2010 using Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter images [2]. The Chang'e-6 INRRI, which reached the Moon in June 2024, is described in its 2025 paper as the first laser retroreflector on the lunar far side [5]. The Turyshev design study of 2013 proposed a single large-aperture cube to replace arrays of small cubes [4].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The arrays are a class of instruments with different designs, sizes and histories. The Apollo, Lunokhod and Chang'e-6 values in this article are tied to named arrays and sources and should not be read as one universal specification. Several numbers differ slightly between sources, for example the Apollo 11 and 14 panel size: 46 cm in the ILRS page and 0.45 m in the UCSD summary table. Masses for the Apollo arrays and the Chang'e-6 INRRI were not verified and are recorded as null. The Turyshev design is a proposal, and the abstract read does not describe a built or flown instrument.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery.

data_quality_notes: Apollo 11, 14 and 15 array masses are null. The Apollo 15 Preliminary Science Report (NASA SP-289, tmurphy.physics.ucsd.edu) was fetched but its scanned PDF text could not be extracted in this run, so its weight table was not read.
Apollo 11 and 14 panel size differs between sources: 46 cm aluminium panel (ILRS page) and 0.45 m square (UCSD summary table). Both are recorded.
Lunokhod panel and cube dimensions are as stated by the UCSD summary table ('each reflector 11 cm per side'); whether 11 cm refers to a triangular face or to the whole reflector is not clarified.
Chang'e-6 INRRI mass and dimensions are null. A secondary search summary gave a mass and size citing an arXiv paper, but that paper was not read, so the figure is not used.
Apollo deployment years are omitted because no fetched source stated them. The Apollo 11 placement date appeared only in a lower-confidence mirror and is not used.
The Apollo 11, 14 and 15 image references on the ILRS page (hq.nasa.gov/alsj archive links) were not verified as direct assets and are not included in the image registry.
The Apollo 15 image asset URL was taken from the NASA Photojournal page's own download link and was not independently downloaded, so direct_image_assets_verified_from_official_pages is set to false.
Search result summaries contained inline citation markers and some unverified claims. Only statements confirmed in fetched pages are used as facts.
No lunar landing-site or location recommendations are included, as deferred by the user.
